title: Testing in .NET -- xUnit, mocking, integration tests, WebApplicationFactory
exp: Testing questions at 4 YOE probe whether you write tests that actually catch regressions, not just tests that exist. This day covers the specific patterns and pitfalls that come up in code review of test code itself.
pts: xUnit is the most common modern .NET testing framework: `[Fact]` for a single test case, `[Theory]` with `[InlineData]`/`[MemberData]` for parametrized tests running the same logic against multiple inputs.

Arrange-Act-Assert (AAA) is the standard test structure -- Arrange sets up inputs and dependencies, Act invokes the method under test exactly once, Assert verifies the outcome. Tests mixing multiple Act steps or asserting mid-arrangement are a common code review flag.

Moq (or NSubstitute) creates mock implementations of interfaces for unit testing in isolation -- `mockRepo.Setup(r => r.GetById(1)).ReturnsAsync(testOrder)` configures the mock's behavior, `mockRepo.Verify(r => r.Save(It.IsAny<Order>()), Times.Once)` asserts a specific interaction occurred.

**Over-mocking** is a real anti-pattern: a test that mocks so many dependencies it no longer tests any real logic, just verifies that mocked methods were called in the expected order -- this couples the test tightly to implementation details and breaks on any refactor, even one that doesn't change behavior.

WebApplicationFactory<TEntryPoint> spins up an in-memory instance of an entire ASP.NET Core application (real middleware pipeline, real DI container, real routing) for integration testing -- HTTP requests are sent in-process without a real network call, but everything else behaves like production.

Test doubles have a spectrum: Dummy (never actually used, just satisfies a parameter), Stub (returns canned data, no verification), Mock (verifies specific interactions occurred), Fake (a lightweight working implementation, like an in-memory database standing in for a real one). Conflating these terms in an interview is a minor but noticeable signal.

EF Core's in-memory provider (`UseInMemoryDatabase`) is convenient for fast tests but does NOT enforce the same constraints as a real relational database (foreign keys, unique constraints, certain LINQ translations) -- a test passing against the in-memory provider is not a guarantee the same code works correctly against SQL Server. SQLite in-memory mode is a closer, though still imperfect, substitute when relational behavior actually matters to the test.

Test data builders (a fluent builder pattern for constructing complex test entities with sensible defaults, only overriding what a specific test cares about) reduce test brittleness compared to constructing a full entity inline in every test method.
pr: Write an over-mocked test, identify why it's fragile, then rewrite it to test behavior instead of implementation details

qa.q: What is over-mocking and why does it make tests worse rather than better?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Over-mocking happens when a test mocks so many of a class's dependencies that the test no longer exercises any real logic -- it just verifies that certain mocked methods were called, in a certain order, with certain arguments. This tightly couples the test to the CURRENT implementation details rather than the class's observable BEHAVIOR, meaning a refactor that preserves correct behavior but changes internal call order or structure breaks the test even though nothing is actually wrong. Tests should verify outcomes and meaningful interactions with true external dependencies, not micromanage every internal call.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** EF Core translates LINQ expression trees into SQL ASTs, executes via ADO.NET, and tracks entity state in the ChangeTracker snapshot dictionary.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** N+1 queries caused by lazy loading in loops result in hundreds of database round-trips and API latency degradation.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** AsNoTracking() boosts read performance by 20-40% and lowers memory usage, but disables automatic update tracking.

qa.q: Why is a passing test against EF Core's in-memory database provider not a guarantee the same code works correctly against SQL Server?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** The in-memory provider doesn't enforce real relational database constraints -- foreign key violations, unique constraints, certain check constraints -- that SQL Server would reject. It also doesn't translate LINQ expressions through the same SQL generation path, so a query using a SQL Server-specific function or a translation edge case could succeed against in-memory but fail or behave differently against the real database. SQLite in-memory mode is a closer substitute since it's an actual relational database with real constraint enforcement, though it still isn't a perfect stand-in for SQL Server-specific behavior.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** T-SQL engine parses, compiles into execution plans, caches them in the plan cache, and executes via the storage engine (buffer pool & latching).

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Parameter sniffing and missing stats cause sub-optimal plan compilation, resulting in full table scans and high CPU.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Parameterization improves plan reuse, but recompile hints (OPTION RECOMPILE) may be needed for skewed data distributions.

qa.q: What is the difference between a Stub, a Mock, and a Fake in test double terminology?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** A Stub returns predetermined canned data when called but the test never verifies HOW it was called -- it's there purely to let the test proceed with known inputs. A Mock additionally records and allows verification of interactions -- the test explicitly asserts a specific method was called a specific number of times with specific arguments. A Fake is a lightweight but genuinely working implementation of the dependency -- an in-memory list standing in for a real database repository, for instance -- that behaves correctly rather than just returning scripted responses. Using the term 'mock' loosely for all three is common in casual conversation but conflating them in a technical interview signals less precision about testing concepts.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Garbage Collector uses generational collection (Gen 0, 1, 2, LOH, POH) with mark-sweep-compact phases. Span<T> provides stack-allocated contiguous representation.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Excessive allocations of large objects (>85KB) trigger frequent Gen 2 / LOH collections, causing GC pause spikes and high CPU.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Span<T> and Memory<T> eliminate heap allocations and copy costs, but ref structs cannot be boxed or captured in async state machines.

qa.q: What does WebApplicationFactory actually spin up, and how does that differ from a pure unit test with mocked dependencies?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** It hosts a real instance of your ASP.NET Core application in-process -- the actual Startup/Program configuration, the real DI container with real service registrations, the real middleware pipeline and routing -- and lets you send HTTP requests to it without a real network call or a separately running process. This is fundamentally different from a unit test with mocked dependencies: it verifies your actual wiring (DI registrations, middleware order, routing configuration) works correctly end-to-end, catching classes of bugs (a missing service registration, a misconfigured middleware order) that pure unit tests with mocks structurally cannot catch, since those tests bypass the real composition root entirely.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** ServiceContainer tracks registration lifetimes (Transient, Scoped, Singleton). Scoped services are tied to an IServiceScope.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Captive dependencies (injecting a Scoped service like DbContext into a Singleton) cause state corruption, memory leaks, and multithreading race conditions.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Explicit scoping ensures request isolation, but requires IServiceScopeFactory for background hosted services.
